title: Looking for advice - local llm
author: AnimeDiff
selftext:
I'm trying to get started building a game in godot with ai with a 4090. I'm trying to use Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct through lmstudio. 

has anyone been using local a llm or other ai models for game dev? in your experience, how does it compare to using codex or another ai API?

I was tinkering around with openclaw but it's very bloated compared to a workflow just for coding. 

now I've moved to vscode + cline. godot-mcp-pro plugin in godot connects well to cline, and the whole setup seems good, but I'm just not getting good results. I also have gdscriot formatter and other related extensions in vscode. not sure if gdscriot is the way to go or godot .net with c#. 

I'm not a coder myself, I'm very good with comfyui, maybe I can use that for asset generation, but working in godot is very foreign to me. still very new to it all, but I see a lot of posts or maybe clickbait of "I made this game entirely with ai.."

what is the best way to actually make a game with ai? 

is there a way for cline or another ai editor to actually interface with godot and build everything properly, hands-free? 

thank you

comments.author: Dependent_Car_3675
comments.body:
I feel you , Godot + AI is a weird combo if you’re new to coding.

My experience:

GDScript is easier than C# for starting.

Use your LLM for boilerplate code, scripts, and functions, but don’t expect it to wire the whole game automatically.

Tools like OpenClaw or Godot-MCP-Pro are nice, but they’re mostly scaffolding. You still need to structure scenes, signals, nodes, etc.

ComfyUI is great for assets, so definitely separate that workflow from coding

Honestly, AI helps a lot, but “entirely AI-made” games you see online usually still require human direction. Treat it as speeding up the coding and prototyping, not hands-free creation.

replies.author: BemaniAK
replies.body: Ask a decent LLM "how do I structure the scenes, nodes and signals to achieve x" and it will usually be able to implement stuff neatly just fine even if you dont know what youre doing yet, it just often cuts whatever corners you don't expressly tell it to not cut, so for newbies that means lots of "is that the best way to do x" re-dos, but you'd be surprised how quick you can learn a lot of best practices this way.

comments.author: HealthyWest6482
comments.body: for coding you'd probably want to look into GPT Plus -> Codex. best bang for buck

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body: I’m doing Godot, codex, cursor, aseprite and pixel lab. I’m new to this but it all is working really well for me! Codex accomplishes what I ask it to after planning for a while like 80% of the time. If it does something wonky I just revert to a backup, and try again explaining the errors and/or word things differently.

comments.author: Due-Height3554
comments.body:
Great advice here already. I'll just add what I learned from building my first AI assisted game (Been programming before AI). ( Also a link here if you want to see the end result --> [https://latepate123.itch.io/cleft-game](https://latepate123.itch.io/cleft-game) ).

The biggest thing is to just start building and forgetting the optimization for now. I did the same thing early on and I just wasted my time. My final workflow ended up being pretty simple: Claude Code + Cline/Opencode + Pixellab for sprites. No fancy MCP, no local models. (Switched from Claude Code to Cline/Opencode when the usage limit filled up). 

But yeah wouldn't say it's hands free and just chilling. But you can absolutely ship a real game without knowing how to code if you're willing to test, give detailed feedback to the AI, and iterate a lot!

The "I made this entirely with AI" posts are real, they just skip over the countless back and forth conversations it took them

comments.author: mrjbelfort
comments.body: I have been trying to use a local LLM not for development but for narration in my game, and personally I don’t think it’s realistic that you could use a local LLM to code. These models are nowhere near powerful enough for it yet. Look into Codex or Claude code

comments.author: Life-Animator-3658
comments.body:
I tried doing local models ran through codex. I have a 4090 and tried the exact model you’re thinking of using. It worked decent, but just bad enough to be extremely frustrating lol. I am a tech lead in my day job. I’ve also been working in Godot for around a decade. 

Local didn’t compare even in the slightest with a 20 dollar subscription to chatGPT. Codex with chatGPT models is amazing. It’s fast, it’s accurate, throw some skill md files in and it’s suddenly coding in the exact style I’ve used for many years. 

I wish the local models worked better. But they just can’t code and call MCP servers reliably. So unless you build your own custom multi model agent, the hassle isn’t worth it.

replies.author: AnimeDiff
replies.body:
I switched over to Claude code through the vscode extension.

It won't work well with cline as cline will use API and charge pay as you go usage, but the vscode extension will use an authorization token and pull from the claud subscription instead. 

It's working perfectly with the godot mcp pro plugin. I started it with a blank project and it's built three connecting scenes, and even built sine wave visualizers. (It's a sort of radio wave  simulator game)

The only downside is how fast it burns through tokens.
